clue.text: Witness catches scoundrel in stable

indicators.note: to catch something is to take hold of it, so one piece closes around another

parts.note: to witness something is to see it
a cur is a contemptible man, a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A witness spots a villain hiding in a stable among the horses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like a building for horses but is the adjective: SEE holds CUR to give SECURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something firmly fixed and not likely to give way is both stable and secure; the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Jumble sale's top stuff bringing little enthusiasm at first

indicators.note: the top of a word written downward is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of sale
to stuff is to cram, pack tightly

indicators.note: 'at first' asks for the opening letter of each of the words it follows

parts.note: the initials of the three words

explanation.surface: At a jumble sale, the best items are snapped up with barely any excitement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumble sale' reads as one phrase, but 'Jumble' alone is the definition, a verb; the 's of 'sale's' joins it to the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To jumble things is to mix them up in a disorderly way, which is what scramble means as a verb.

clue.text: Deal with vote against covering face

parts.note: a con is an argument or vote against, as in pros and cons
the face of a building is its front

explanation.surface: Someone handles a hostile vote while masking their true expression.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'covering' just places the first piece above the second; nothing goes inside anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To confront a problem is to face up to it and tackle it, which is to deal with it.

clue.text: Turned off

definitions.meaning: first meaning: gone sour, as milk turns
second meaning: gone bad, no longer fit to eat

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as switched off or repelled, but each word separately describes food that has spoiled.
explanation.definitionFit: Butter or milk that has turned or gone off smells stale and sour, which is exactly what rancid describes.

clue.text: New notices in areas of potential trouble

parts.note: hot news is new, fresh off the press
to notice something is to spot it

explanation.surface: Fresh warnings have been posted in districts where unrest is expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notices' looks like a noun for posted warnings but works as the verb spots.
explanation.definitionFit: Places of likely conflict or danger are called hot spots, a standard idiom for trouble zones.

clue.text: Eject Jack from tournament

indicators.note: taking something from a larger whole leaves the rest behind

parts.note: a joust is a knightly tournament
J is the card abbreviation for jack

explanation.surface: A player called Jack is thrown out of a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests removing a person named Jack; really it is J taken off JOUST.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone is to force them out of a place or position, so it is a synonym for eject.

clue.text: Succeeded without drugs to become absolutely clean

parts.note: s. is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies
pot is slang for cannabis
less means lacking or without, as in sugarless

explanation.surface: Someone kicked a drug habit and is now completely clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clean' in the surface means drug-free; in the definition it means free of dirt. 'Without' becomes LESS placed after the drugs, not a deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with no marks or stains at all is spotless, entirely and perfectly clean.

clue.text: Choose not to get involved with solicitor after work

indicators.note: one thing coming after another follows it, so this sets the order of the two parts

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work
a tout solicits custom, such as a ticket tout

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to get mixed up with a lawyer after hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solicitor' looks like a British lawyer but here is anyone who solicits business: a TOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To opt out is to decide to withdraw from or not take part in an arrangement, so to stay uninvolved.

clue.text: Plants found in south facing borders

indicators.note: to face something is to stand up against it, so the parts are placed side by side

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
borders are edges

explanation.surface: A gardener notes which plants grow in the south-facing flowerbeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facing' just puts one piece against the next. 'Borders' in the surface are flowerbeds, a gardening sense, but they give EDGES.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedges are grasslike plants of damp ground, so they are an example of plants.

clue.text: Arguments caused by knight sharing spoils

indicators.note: to share something is to let another piece into its space, so one goes inside the other

parts.note: to spoil something is to ruin it
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: A knight's quarrels arise over dividing the plunder of battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' looks like loot taken in war but is the verb ruins. Chess uses N for knight because K is the king.
explanation.definitionFit: A run-in is an informal word for a quarrel or clash with someone, so a plural synonym for arguments.

clue.text: Classified ad featuring exotic escorts about to be removed

indicators.note: a thing that features something includes it within itself
exotic means strange and foreign, so the letters take an unfamiliar order
something removed is taken out, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
c. is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A small advert in the paper offers foreign escorts for hire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classified ad' reads as a newspaper small ad, but 'Classified' alone is the definition, and the ad is split open to hold the rest. 'About' is c., circa.
explanation.definitionFit: Assorted goods have been sorted into kinds or groups, which is what classified means.

clue.text: Happen to get new suspect-tracing aid — it's an advantage

parts.note: to be is to exist or take place, as in 'so be it'
N is the abbreviation for new
an e-fit is a computer-built likeness of a suspect, used by British police

explanation.surface: Police luck into a fresh identikit picture, which helps the investigation.
explanation.walkthrough: An E-FIT is the electronic successor to the Photofit, an image assembled from a witness's description.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefit is a helpful or favourable factor, so it is a near synonym of advantage.

clue.text: Strict disciplinarian's right to set about wayward inmate? Just the opposite

indicators.note: to set one thing about another is to place it around the other
this reverses the roles just stated, so the outer and inner parts swap places
wayward means wandering off course, so the letters stray from their order

parts.note: taken as written
RT is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A harsh prison officer is entitled to rough up an unruly prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, RT goes around the jumbled INMATE; 'Just the opposite' flips it so the jumbled INMATE goes around RT. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a person who insists on rigid obedience to rules, named after a strict French drillmaster.

clue.text: Appeal from injured guerilla American soldier ignored

indicators.note: an injured body is knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
something ignored is left out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a GI is a US army soldier

explanation.surface: A wounded rebel fighter pleads for help while a US soldier walks past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appeal' looks like a plea for help but is the noun meaning attraction. Remove G and I from GUERILLA, then rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Allure is the quality of being attractive or tempting, which is the sense of appeal as charm.

clue.text: Justify the rise of crude bombast

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: crude means raw, unrefined
a rant is loud, overblown talk

explanation.surface: Someone defends the growing popularity of crude, loud rhetoric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' sounds like growing popularity, but in a down clue it turns the word for crude upside down; the noun for bombast then follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To warrant an action is to give good grounds for it, so to justify it; the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Unlikely to happen as principal leaves hurriedly

indicators.note: whatever leaves goes away, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: to rush headlong is to go hurriedly
a principal is the head of a school

explanation.surface: A head teacher dashing out of school is a rare sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves hurriedly' looks like a description of the principal rushing out; it is HEAD leaving HEADLONG.
explanation.definitionFit: Long odds are given on an outcome considered improbable, so a long chance is one unlikely to come off.

clue.text: Since coming from Belgium Hercule finally with grounds for action

parts.note: B is the international vehicle code for Belgium

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word it goes with

parts.note: the closing letter of Hercule
a cause is a reason or legal ground for a lawsuit

explanation.surface: Hercule Poirot, the Belgian detective, finally has the motive he needs to act.
explanation.walkthrough: Hercule Poirot is Agatha Christie's Belgian sleuth, which makes 'Since coming from Belgium' look like his backstory.
explanation.definitionFit: Since and because are both conjunctions introducing a reason, as in 'since you asked'.

clue.text: Agree to meet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to correspond or be in accord
second meaning: to occupy the same place or time

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as consenting to a meeting, but the two verbs are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Opinions that match are said to coincide, and two events or lines occurring together also coincide.

clue.text: Play the part of Obama spurning soldiers with quick reply

parts.note: to come the hero is British slang for acting the part of one

indicators.note: to spurn is to reject, so those letters are thrown out

parts.note: Barack is Obama's first name
RA is the Royal Artillery, British gunners

explanation.surface: An actor impersonating Obama snubs the troops but has a sharp answer ready.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come' meaning to act a role is British informal usage, as in 'don't come the innocent with me'. Obama stands for his first name, not his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A comeback is a witty or cutting retort, so it is a quick reply.

clue.text: Reportedly uninjured after rush to find refuge from danger

parts.note: to bolt is to dash off

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so what counts is how it is said

parts.note: whole means unharmed, intact

explanation.surface: Survivors, said to be unhurt, dash for shelter from the threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the sound of whole after the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolthole is a hideaway one can escape to when in trouble, so a place of refuge.

clue.text: Weapon found in ditch brought back by petty officer

parts.note: PO is the naval abbreviation for petty officer

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so it runs backwards

parts.note: a ditch is a drain for water

explanation.surface: A naval officer retrieves a weapon discovered in a ditch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' means beside, so the reversed ditch sits next to the officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A poniard is a small slim dagger, so it is an example of a weapon.

clue.text: Fool with Dickens over …

parts.note: Boz was the pen name of Charles Dickens
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: The ellipsis carries on into the next clue, as if a fool were spending time with Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens signed his early Sketches by Boz with that name. The ellipsis ties the surface to 25 across but has no role in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Bozo is a slang American term for a stupid or clownish person, so a synonym of fool.

clue.text: Barker, perhaps set up after denunciation, gets put in prison

parts.note: a ban is a formal curse or condemnation

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting something up raises it, so it reads from the bottom

parts.note: a pug is a dog, an example of a barker

explanation.surface: Ronnie Barker, framed after being denounced, ends up behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronnie Barker played the convict Fletcher in the British prison sitcom Porridge, which makes the surface feel apt. 'After' places the raised dog after BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Bang up is British slang for locking someone in a cell, so it means to put in prison.

clue.text: It provides excitement say in spring

definitions.meaning: first meaning: whatever supplies something, with excitement given as one example
second meaning: the place where a river rises from the ground

explanation.surface: Something brings a thrill in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season; it is the wellspring of a river. 'Say' marks excitement as only one thing that might be provided.
explanation.definitionFit: A source is the origin that supplies something, such as a source of excitement, and also the spring a stream issues from.

clue.text: Faultless from rookie

parts.note: the -less ending of this word means having none
a vice is a fault or failing in character

explanation.walkthrough: The one word is read in two parts with the order swapped: its ending comes first, then its stem, as a phrase meaning without fault.
explanation.definitionFit: A rookie is a beginner new to a job, and a novice is a learner or newcomer; the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: … the full effect of Abbot's debut on stage

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of Abbot
to stage a play is to mount it

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, a fool feels the full force of a comic's first stage appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' looks like a theatre noun but is the verb mount. Read with 21 across, the fool and Abbot evoke the comedy duo Abbott and Costello.
explanation.definitionFit: Amount can mean the total sum or whole significance of something, as when a remark amounts to an insult.

clue.text: Suspect in stolen lippy

indicators.note: a suspect account is dubious and unreliable, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A suspect is caught carrying a pilfered lipstick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lippy' looks like slang for lipstick, which is how the surface uses it; it is the adjective for cheeky.
explanation.definitionFit: Lippy is informal British for cheekily disrespectful in speech, which is what insolent means.

clue.text: Involving amateurs rising within officialdom

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from bottom to top
within says the letters sit inside the word that follows

parts.note: a run of letters in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: Amateurs are climbing the ranks of the bureaucracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising within' reads as a career climb, but it says the letters lie inside the long word and read upwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Laic means relating to the laity, people who are not clergy, the lay or non-professional people.

clue.text: Novel in the earliest stage of development

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Zola's novel of a French mining strike

definitions.text: in the earliest stage of development
definitions.meaning: second meaning: just sprouting, like a seed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the adjective meaning new, which fits the rest; it is a book title by Émile Zola.
explanation.definitionFit: Germinal describes something at the germ or seed stage, barely begun; it is also the title of Zola's 1885 novel.

clue.text: Success after Rushdie's first to break through for UK publisher

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it

parts.note: via means by way of, through

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word it goes with

parts.note: the opening letter of Rushdie
to make a go of something is to succeed at it

explanation.surface: A British publishing house finally has a hit once Salman Rushdie makes his breakthrough.
explanation.walkthrough: Virago Press is a London publisher of books by women, so it sits naturally beside a novelist in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Virago is a British publishing imprint founded in 1973, so the name is that of a UK publisher.

clue.text: Republican VP hedging about the end of his political influence

indicators.note: a hedge surrounds a field, so hedging puts a boundary around something

parts.note: Mike Pence was the Republican vice-president under Trump
re means about, concerning

indicators.note: the end of a word is its closing letter

parts.note: the closing letter of his

explanation.surface: A vice-president equivocates about the end of his own clout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hedging' looks like evasive talk but is the container signal. 'Republican' only describes the VP; it gives no R.
explanation.definitionFit: A country's military or political presence is the influence it exerts somewhere by being felt there.

clue.text: Outrageous cheek without unqualified driver getting to shout abusively

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps another
outrageous behaviour is wildly out of line, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
L is the learner plate on a car driven by someone without a licence

explanation.surface: An unlicensed motorist with appalling cheek yells at other road users.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking, but here it has its older meaning outside: the jumbled letters sit around L.
explanation.definitionFit: To heckle is to interrupt a speaker with jeers and insults, so to shout abusively at them.
